## Margin of Error

A good confidence interval balances **precision** with **uncertainty**


::: {.incremental .large}

- The temperature tomorrow will be between -100 $^\circ F$ and 150 $^\circ F$    
[**Uncertainty, no precision**]{.fragment .emph  .blue-dk}<br/><br/>


- Jake will win over Amy with a spread of between 3.40928 and 3.40948    
[**Precision, no uncertainty/unreasonable certainty**]{.fragment .emph  .blue-dk}<br/><br/>

- I expect I'll get between 6.5 and 8 hours of sleep tonight    
[**Reasonable precision and uncertainty**]{.fragment .emph  .blue-dk}<br/>
    
:::


## Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval is constructed using the form:

[Estimate $\pm$ Multiplier $\times$ Standard Error]{.large}

Each confidence interval has a **level** determined by the multiplier

::: {.r-stack}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-extra: ".fragment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
x <- seq(-3, 3, .01)
df <- tibble(x = x, y = dnorm(x))
df_shaded <- filter(df, abs(x)<= 1.96)
df_unshaded <- anti_join(df, df_shaded)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_line() + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3)
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-extra: ".fragment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_shaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0), fill = "#f16278", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line() + 
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.1, label = "95% area") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96) + 
  annotate("text", x = -1.96, y = 0.2, label = "z = -1.96", hjust = 1.1) + 
  annotate("text", x =  1.96, y = 0.2, label = "z =  1.96", hjust = -0.1) + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3)
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-extra: ".fragment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_shaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0), fill = "#f16278", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_unshaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0, group = sign(x)), fill = "#1a5c7f", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line() + 
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.1, label = "95% area") + 
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 0, label = "2.5% area", hjust = 1) + 
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 0, label = "2.5% area", hjust = 0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96) + 
  annotate("text", x = -1.96, y = 0.2, label = "z = -1.96", hjust = 1.1) + 
  annotate("text", x =  1.96, y = 0.2, label = "z =  1.96", hjust = -0.1) + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3)

```

:::


[A 95% confidence interval will use a multiplier of 1.96]{.fragment}

::: fragment

```{r}
#| echo: true
qnorm(.975)
```
:::


## Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval is constructed using the form:

[Estimate $\pm$ Multiplier $\times$ Standard Error]{.large}

Each confidence interval has a **level** determined by the multiplier

::: {.r-stack}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-extra: ".fragment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
x <- seq(-3, 3, .01)
df <- tibble(x = x, y = dnorm(x))
df_shaded <- filter(df, abs(x)<= qnorm(.995))
df_unshaded <- anti_join(df, df_shaded)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_line() + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3)
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-extra: ".fragment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_shaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0), fill = "#f16278", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line() + 
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.1, label = "99% area") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.995)) + 
  annotate("text", x = -qnorm(.995), y = 0.2, label = "z = -2.58", hjust = 1.1) + 
  annotate("text", x =  qnorm(.995), y = 0.2, label = "z =  2.58", hjust = -0.1) + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3)
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-extra: ".fragment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_shaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0), fill = "#f16278", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_unshaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0, group = sign(x)), fill = "#1a5c7f", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line() + 
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.1, label = "99% area") + 
  annotate("text", x = -qnorm(.995), y = 0.05, label = "0.5% area", hjust = 1) + 
  annotate("text", x = qnorm(.995), y = 0.05, label = "0.5% area", hjust = 0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.995)) + 
  annotate("text", x = -qnorm(.995), y = 0.2, label = "z = -2.58", hjust = 1.1) + 
  annotate("text", x =  qnorm(.995), y = 0.2, label = "z =  2.58", hjust = -0.1) + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3)

```

:::


[A 99% confidence interval will use a multiplier of `{r} qnorm(.995)`]{.fragment}

::: fragment

```{r}
#| echo: true
qnorm(.995)
```
:::

## What does "95% confident" mean?

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: A set of 100 horizontal lines representing the lower and upper bounds of a confidence interval, with the sample mean marked as a dot. Intervals are sorted vertically by lower bound. Intervals containing the true population parameter of 3 are colored grey, intervals which do not contain the true parameter value are colored red; there are 2 intervals near the bottom and 3 at the top which do not contain the true parameter.

set.seed(36044347)
true_mean <- 3
sim <- tibble(i = 1:100, sample = replicate(100, list(rnorm(30, true_mean, sd = 1)))) |>
  mutate(sample_mean = map_dbl(sample, mean), sample_se = map_dbl(sample, sd)/sqrt(30), 
         lb = sample_mean - qnorm(.975)*sample_se, 
         ub = sample_mean + qnorm(.975)*sample_se, 
         contains_true = lb < true_mean & ub > true_mean) |>
  arrange(sample_mean) |>
  mutate(j = 1:n())

ggplot(sim) + 
  geom_linerange(aes(y = j, xmin = lb, xmax = ub, color = contains_true)) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = sample_mean, y = j)) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean) + 
  scale_color_manual("Contains\npopulation\nparameter", values = c("red", "grey40")) + 
  theme(legend.position.inside = c(.15, .85), legend.position = "inside") + 
  xlab("Sample Mean") + ylab("Iteration (sorted by sample mean)") + 
  ggtitle("Monte Carlo Confidence Intervals")
```
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
- If we took 100 different samples of the same size,     
95 of the intervals should contain the true mean

::: fragment
["95% confident" does NOT mean:]{.emph .large .cerulean-dk}
:::

::: incremental

- **95% probability** that the interval contains the true value    
[95% is the [**long run**]{.emph .large .pink-dk} behavior of the method]{.fragment}    
[(Use Bayesian methods for this interpretation -- take a Bayesian course for more info)]{.small .fragment}    
<br/>

- 95% of the **sample observations** lie within the interval    
[CIs are for [**population**]{.emph .large .pink-dk} values estimated by a [**statistic**]{.emph .large .pink-dk}]{.fragment}    
<br/>

- **95% of future sample means** will fall within this interval    
[A [**prediction interval**]{.emph .large .pink-dk} (diff. calc.) is used for future values]{.fragment}

:::

:::
:::


## Testing a Hypothesis

::: columns

::: column

Someone proposed that 50% of people on the internet are actually dogs. 

![](../slides/images/internet-dog.jpg){fig-alt="A picture of a dog wearing glasses and using a computer, with the caption 'on the internet, nobody knows you're a dog'."}


You construct a CAT-Cha test to identify internet users who are dogs, and discover that of 100 internet users tested, 35 are dogs. 

:::
::: column
::: fragment
$$\begin{align}\overline X &= \frac{35}{100} = 0.35\\\\
\text{SE}[X] &= \sqrt{\frac{.35(.65)}{100}} = 0.0477\end{align}$$
:::

::: fragment
$$\begin{align}\overline X \pm 1.96\cdot \text{SE}[\overline X] &= .35 \pm 1.96 \cdot 0.0477 \\&= (0.257, 0.443)\end{align}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .large}
<br/>    
0.5 is not in (0.257, 0.443) $\Rightarrow$ 
:::

::: {.fragment .large}
$p$ = 0.5 is not a plausible value for the proportion of dogs on the internet
:::


:::
:::




## Testing a Hypothesis

::: columns

::: column

Someone proposed that 50% of people on the internet are actually dogs. 

![](../slides/images/internet-dog.jpg){fig-alt="A picture of a dog wearing glasses and using a computer, with the caption 'on the internet, nobody knows you're a dog'."}


You construct a CAT-Cha test to identify internet users who are dogs, and discover that of 100 internet users tested, 35 are dogs. 

:::
::: column

::: fragment
$$\begin{align}H_0&: \mu = 0.50\\
H_A&: \mu \neq 0.50\end{align}$$
:::

::: fragment
$$\begin{align}\overline X &= \frac{35}{100} = 0.35\\\\
\text{SE}[X] &= \sqrt{\frac{.35(.65)}{100}} = 0.0477\end{align}$$
:::


::: fragment
$$\begin{align}Z^\ast &= \frac{\overline X - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{N}} \approx \frac{\overline X - \mu}{\text{SE}[\overline X]}\\& = \frac{0.35 - 0.5}{0.0477} = -3.145
\end{align}$$
:::

::: fragment
```{r}
x <- seq(-4, 4, .01)
df <- tibble(x = x, y = dnorm(x))
df_shaded <- filter(df, abs(x)<= 3.145)
df_unshaded <- anti_join(df, df_shaded)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = df_unshaded, aes(ymax = y, ymin = 0, group = sign(x)), fill = "#1a5c7f", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line() + 
  annotate("text", x = -3.145, y = 0.02, label = "0.08% area", hjust = 1) + 
  annotate("text", x = 3.145, y = 0.02, label = "0.08% area", hjust = 0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * 3.145) + 
  annotate("text", x = -3.145, y = 0.2, label = "z = -3.145", hjust = 1.1) + 
  annotate("text", x =  3.145, y = 0.2, label = "z =  3.145", hjust = -0.1) + 
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Z") + ggtitle("Normal Distribution") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -4:4)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .large}
We [**reject $H_0$**]{.emph .cerulean-dk} that $p=0.50$ with probability $p = 0.0016$ and [**conclude that it is more likely that the proportion of dogs on the internet is not 50%**]{.emph .cerulean-dk}, given the data that we have observed. 
:::


:::
:::
